subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 34-year-old woman presents with 1 year of progressive fatigue and exertional dyspnea. Her menstrual periods last 7 days and require double protection. She has begun chewing several cups of ice daily and notes that her nails have become spoon-shaped and brittle. Examination shows pale conjunctivae, angular cheilitis, and koilonychia. Hemoglobin is 9.0 g/dL with an MCV of 71 fL and an increased red cell distribution width.
question: Which of the following patterns of iron studies is most likely in this patient?

options.text: Decreased serum iron, decreased total iron-binding capacity, increased ferritin
Decreased serum iron, increased total iron-binding capacity, decreased ferritin
Increased serum iron, decreased total iron-binding capacity, increased ferritin
Increased serum iron, increased total iron-binding capacity, decreased ferritin
Normal serum iron, normal total iron-binding capacity, increased ferritin

explanation_correct: Chronic menstrual blood loss depletes iron stores, so ferritin, the storage protein and the best single indicator of total body iron, is low and serum iron falls. Transferrin (measured as total iron-binding capacity) is increased because hepatic transferrin synthesis rises when iron stores are low, and the resulting microcytic, hypochromic anemia with an elevated red cell distribution width, pica, and koilonychia completes the classic picture.

explanation_incorrect.A: A low total iron-binding capacity with a high ferritin indicates anemia of chronic disease or inflammation rather than iron deficiency.
explanation_incorrect.C: This pattern is typical of hereditary hemochromatosis or other iron-overload states, in which transferrin saturation is high, not low.
explanation_incorrect.D: An elevated serum iron makes iron deficiency implausible, and no common condition produces this combination.
explanation_incorrect.E: A normal serum iron with a high ferritin suggests acute phase response or early inflammation, not iron deficiency with pica and koilonychia.

educationalObjective: Iron deficiency anemia shows low ferritin, low serum iron, and elevated total iron-binding capacity, and it causes pica and koilonychia.
